titre: Candela Pours a 1.5 cm Roof for Cosmic Rays
accroche: In 1951 in Mexico City, Félix Candela pours a concrete roof 1.5 centimeters thick, thin enough to let the cosmic rays to be measured pass through.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1951, the National University of Mexico sets up a laboratory in Mexico City to measure cosmic rays, those particles from space that constantly pass through Earth's atmosphere. The specifications impose an unusual constraint for a roof: it must be thin enough not to slow these particles before they reach the detectors installed beneath. The engineer in charge of the project, the Spanish exile Félix Candela, a former captain of engineers in the Republican army who has been a refugee in Mexico since 1939, pours a concrete shell 1.5 centimeters thick at its thinnest point: the thickness of two stacked coins.

## A Shell, Not a Wall

A concrete roof this thin should not normally stand: laid flat, on a simple slab, it would collapse under its own weight before carrying anything else. Candela makes it stand by curving it into a ruled geometry, the hyperbolic paraboloid: a saddle-shaped surface, hollowed in one direction and bulging in the other. This double curvature distributes loads within the thickness of the shell itself rather than making them bear on beams, just as an eggshell resists pressure despite its negligible thickness. Although the form looks sculpted from curves, every hyperbolic paraboloid is built with perfectly straight formwork boards, laid out in a fan: the curvature arises from their assembly, not from the wood itself. The cosmic ray pavilion, nicknamed “La Muela” (the molar) for its silhouette, is the fourth shell built by Cubiertas Ala, the company Candela has just founded with his brother and sister, but the first in which it uses the hyperbolic paraboloid. This geometry makes Candela's reputation.

## What This Shifts

Concrete has a reputation as a heavy material, one that stands by the mass piled up. The cosmic ray pavilion demonstrates the opposite: it is the form, not the quantity of material, that carries the structure. In the following years Cubiertas Ala will build several hundred shells on this principle across Mexico, up to the Los Manantiales restaurant in Xochimilco, in 1958, whose shell, 4 centimeters thick, still shelters diners today beneath four interlocking hyperbolic paraboloids. An engineer who had fled a war for the thinness of a wall becomes, within a few years, the author of the lightest roofing in the country that took him in.

repere.texte: The cosmic ray pavilion built by Félix Candela at the National University of Mexico in 1951 has a concrete shell 1.5 centimeters thick at its thinnest point, covering 12 meters by 10.75 meters: thin enough to let through the particles the laboratory was to measure.

carte.punch: Candela poured a 1.5 cm concrete roof to let cosmic rays through.
carte.idee: In 1951, for a cosmic ray laboratory in Mexico City, Félix Candela pours a concrete shell 1.5 centimeters thick. It stands thanks to its double curvature, a hyperbolic paraboloid, and not through the mass of the material: the form carries the structure, not the thickness.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: El Pabellón de Rayos Cósmicos cumple 50 años, Gaceta UNAM
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full story of the pavilion, from its scientific construction in 1951 to its conversion under the care of the School of Dentistry.

quiz.question: How can a concrete roof only 1.5 centimeters thick stand without collapsing?
choix: It rests entirely on a network of pillars spaced two meters apart
It is reinforced by a steel mesh so dense that it compensates for the thinness of the concrete
The concrete used is a special alloy, stronger than ordinary concrete
Its double saddle-shaped curvature distributes loads within the thickness of the concrete, like an eggshell
quiz.explication: The double curvature of the hyperbolic paraboloid distributes stresses within the thickness of the concrete itself, like an eggshell; neither a dense steel mesh, nor closely spaced pillars, nor a special concrete explains how this 1.5-centimeter shell holds.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who is Félix Candela before becoming the author of the cosmic ray pavilion?
choix: A Mexican mathematics professor specializing in statistics
A captain of engineers in the Spanish Republican army, a refugee in Mexico since 1939
An American engineer sent to Mexico by the University of Chicago
A former Mexican mason turned self-taught architect
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Candela is a former captain of engineers in the Spanish Republican army, in exile in Mexico since 1939 after the civil war.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How are the formwork boards used to build the curvature of the hyperbolic paraboloid?
choix: They are pre-curved with steam before being set up on the site
They are replaced by flexible metal sheets that follow the shape
They are perfectly straight but laid out in a fan, the curvature arising from their assembly
They are poured directly into the concrete and never removed
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Each hyperbolic paraboloid is built with straight formwork boards, laid out in a fan: the curvature arises from their assembly, not from the wood.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the Los Manantiales restaurant, built by Cubiertas Ala in 1958?
choix: A shell 4 centimeters thick formed of four interlocking hyperbolic paraboloids
The very first building constructed by Candela's company in Mexico
A scientific laboratory with an even thinner roof than the 1951 pavilion
A building left unfinished after Candela left the company
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Los Manantiales, in Xochimilco, has a shell 4 centimeters thick made of four interlocking hyperbolic paraboloids.
